```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"

```

```{r setup}
library(transmap)
data(transmap_example)
```

`transmap` builds program phenotypes; association testing, fine-mapping and
colocalization are done with other tools. This vignette shows how program
phenotypes fit into a *trans*-QTL analysis, and the design choices that keep
the analysis valid.

# 1. A simulated *trans* effect

We simulate genotypes for 200 variants on chromosome 5 and add a *trans* effect
of one variant, `chr5:50000`, on the genes of the first simulated module.

```{r simulate}
set.seed(1)
Y <- transmap_example$Y
n <- nrow(Y)
p <- 200
G <- sapply(runif(p, 0.05, 0.5), function(f) rbinom(n, 2, f))
dimnames(G) <- list(rownames(Y), sprintf("chr5:%d", seq_len(p) * 1000))
causal <- "chr5:50000"
module_1 <- transmap_example$modules$module_1
Y[, module_1] <- Y[, module_1] + 0.3 * as.numeric(scale(G[, causal]))
```

# 2. Build program phenotypes

```{r programs}
loc <- transmap_local(Y, transmap_example$modules,
                      null_z = transmap_example$null_z,
                      covariates = transmap_example$covariates)
colnames(loc$scores)
```

# 3. Marginal association scan

The phenotypes are ordinary quantitative outcomes. A simple marginal scan
computes, for every variant and phenotype, the z-score of the correlation
test:

```{r scan}
assoc_z <- function(G, P) {
  r <- cor(G, P)
  r * sqrt(nrow(G) - 2) / sqrt(1 - r^2)
}
Z <- assoc_z(G, loc$scores)
dim(Z)
top <- apply(abs(Z), 2, which.max)
data.frame(phenotype = colnames(Z),
           top_variant = rownames(Z)[top],
           abs_z = round(apply(abs(Z), 2, max), 2))
```

The first whitened component of `module_1` has its strongest association at
the simulated causal variant. In real analyses, use a dedicated QTL mapping
tool (for example, tensorQTL or QTLtools) with the program phenotypes as the
phenotype matrix, and adjust for covariates either there or through the
`covariates` argument of `transmap_local()` and `transmap_global()`.

# 4. Leave-one-chromosome-out

A variant can affect genes on its own chromosome in *cis*. If those genes are
part of a program, a *cis* effect can appear as a *trans* effect on the
program. To avoid this, build the phenotypes used to test variants on a
chromosome from genes on other chromosomes only:

```{r loco, eval = FALSE}
# gene_chr: chromosome of every column of Y
for (chr in paste0("chr", 1:22)) {
  Y_chr <- Y[, gene_chr != chr]
  hs_chr <- r_hotspot(Y_chr)
  loc_chr <- transmap_local(Y_chr, hs_chr, null_z = null_z,
                            covariates = covariates)
  # map variants on `chr` against loc_chr$scores
}
```

For TransMap-global, the `exclude` argument of `r_transcca()` masks variant-gene
pairs on the same chromosome, and the statistics can be subset to other
chromosomes before building `data_list` (see
[Constructing the W Matrix](Constructing_W_Matrix.html)).

# 5. Avoiding selection bias for global programs

Global programs are chosen because their genes associate with particular
variants. Testing the same variants for association with the same program in
the same samples reuses that information, and the resulting p-values are too
small. Learn the programs and test their phenotypes on independent data, for
example:

- split the samples, learn programs with `r_transcca()` in one part and score
  and map them with `transmap_global()` in the other;
- learn programs from one set of chromosomes and map variants on the others.

```{r split, eval = FALSE}
set.seed(1)
idx <- sample(nrow(Y), nrow(Y) / 2)
# learn programs in the first half
prog <- r_transcca(list(G = scale(G[idx, ]), E = scale(Y[idx, ])),
                   K = 2, sumabs = 0.25)
# score and map them in the second half
glob <- transmap_global(Y[-idx, ], prog)
Z_global <- assoc_z(G[-idx, ], glob$scores)
```

Local programs are built from expression and null *trans* z-scores, not from
the associations of the variants being tested, so they are not selected for
association with those variants.

# 6. Fine-mapping and colocalization

Program phenotypes can be fine-mapped like any other quantitative trait, for
example with `susieR`:

```{r susie, eval = FALSE}
library(susieR)
fit <- susie(X = G, y = loc$scores[, "module_1_WPC1"], L = 10)
fit$sets$cs
```

Because each scale gives a different view of the same *trans* effect, the
phenotypes can be analysed jointly by multi-trait colocalization, for example
with [ColocBoost](https://statfungen.github.io/colocboost/), to find variants
shared across *cis*-eGenes, *trans*-eGenes and *trans* programs:

```{r colocboost, eval = FALSE}
library(colocboost)
# Phenotypes from all scales, for the same samples as the genotypes G
traits <- cbind(Y[, module_1], loc$scores)
res <- colocboost(X = G, Y = traits)
```

For summary statistics from large cohorts, both tools also accept z-scores with
an LD reference instead of individual-level data.
